title: An overwhelming fraction of non-simple rules are universal

fields.label: Label
fields.value: An overwhelming fraction of non-simple rules are universal

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Among all possible rules of a given type (such as cellular automata) whose behavior is not obviously simple, i.e. not repetitive or nested, the overwhelming majority are computationally universal, so universality is extremely common rather than a rare engineered property.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: among all possible systems with behavior that is not obviously simple an overwhelming fraction are universal.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 12, “The Principle of Computational Equivalence”; section “The Content of the Principle” (from p. 719), p. 721. Scope: enumerable classes of simple programs such as cellular automata, Turing machines and related systems

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch12-04: needs-new-data, resolvability 0.35

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Available enumerations allow bounded estimates but leave many members unclassified. The asserted overwhelming fraction and cross-family scope require major new mathematical results and explicit measures.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For each precisely defined rule family and size distribution, classify obvious simplicity and prove or disprove universality for the remaining rules, then calculate the asymptotic universal fraction.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
No canonical distribution exists over all possible rules.

Behavioral non-simplicity does not itself certify universality.

Universality is undecidable in broad families.

fields.value:

data adequacy: 0.15

operationalizability: 0.45

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: One can separate many obviously simple rules by proof or by exhaustive simulation, and one can list the few non-simple rules already proved universal. That is a lower bound and a classification of the complement's appearance, not a density of universality. No published argument currently computes, or even bounds, the overwhelming fraction the claim asserts.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: On each finite family of rules, remove those with a proved repetitive or nested form and estimate the fraction of the remainder that emulate a Turing machine. An overwhelming fraction, in a limit that is specified in advance, would confirm the claim; a positive-density set of non-simple, non-universal rules would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The density has to be taken over a stated sequence of finite families; different limits can disagree.

Universality of a typical rule is not settled by inspecting a finite evolution, so behavior censuses do not estimate the fraction.
